newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Singh says budget euphoria may fizzle out.
newsitem.headline: India's Singh says budget euphoria may fizzle out.

text.p: Former finance minister Manmohan Singh has said India's federal budget for 1997/98 gave a shot in the arm to faltering business confidence but the euphoria could be short-lived.
In an interview published in the Business Standard newspaper on Sunday, Singh said Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's budget had cheered the morale of industrialists and capital markets.
"And I compliment the finance minister for doing this," Singh said. "But it cannot last if the fundamentals have any active role to play."

Chidambaram on Friday cut taxes and slashed import duties in the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1. In two special trading sessions after the announcements, Indian stocks surged around 10 percent.

"All the euphoria this budget has created will come to nothing if this government does not have the nerve to tackle the problem of the yawning deficit in the oil pool account," Singh said. The oil pool deficit is expected to hit 158 billion rupees ($4.4 billion) by the end of March.
Singh said the budget's assumption that tax and non-tax revenues would rise 16 to 17 percent in 1997/98 assumed an economic growth rate of seven to eight percent.
He said if one superimposed a 12 percent railway hike, announced last week, and a possibile adjustment in the oil pool account, inflation could be a major problem.

"The 8.0 percent inflation rate for the second year in a row sends wrong signals. It will introduce social unrest, it is not good for the long-run management of the country," he said, adding India should work towards a five percent inflation rate.
Singh -- the architect of a reforms programme that has driven India's gradual conversion to a free-market economy since 1991 -- said Chidambaram's tax package was well defined.
But he did not agree with the move to cut income tax rates to below 40 percent. "In a poor country, a 40 percent tax rate is the right way to work," he said.
Singh said if a widely-expected oil price hike had been announced in the budget, the country would have received a clearer picture.
"Now tomorrow, if there is an oil price adjustment, the people will feel cheated. People would have second thoughts about all the euphoria," he said.
"Confidence is really a fickle thing -- it takes very long to build and very little time to destroy."
